items.title: The living world is forcing scientists to rethink purpose
items.description:
Alan Love studies how scientists think about life, purpose, and agency. In this full interview, he offers a wide-ranging guide to purpose in living systems, moving across biology, medicine, artificial intelligence, and the structure of science itself. He explores what it means for organisms to act with direction, why agency matters at multiple scales, and how ideas like function and goal-directed behavior can help us better understand life.

items.title: The invisible forces that create talent and elite performance
items.description:
Talent isn’t a gift we’re born with – it’s a signal we’ve been reading completely wrong. Author Daniel Coyle breaks down the common traits shared by successful people, and why environment, not innate ability, is the variable that ties them all together. 
 
 This video  The invisible forces that create talent and elite performance   is featured on  Big Think .

items.title: New video: Largest-scale cosmic test ever favors dark matter over MOND
items.description: Anytime there’s a chance to subject our Universe to a new cosmic test, it’s imperative that we do it. First off, it gives the Universe a chance to surprise us: to show us something that we never could have learned unless we looked. Second off, it gives us a chance to test our underlying assumptions about the Universe: what it’s made of, what laws and rules it obeys, and how it behaves in never-before-probed ways. items.title: The world’s greatest mathematician explains 6 essential concepts of math
items.description:
Terence Tao has spent decades solving problems most people can’t even state, and he says he’s never had a single eureka moment. In this conversation, the UCLA mathematician and Fields Medalist breaks math down to six essential ideas: numbers, algebra, geometry, probability, analysis, and dynamics. 
 
 This video  The world’s greatest mathematician explains 6 essential concepts of math  is featured on  Big Think .

items.title: The sky is blue. The ocean is, too. But the reasons why are very different.
items.description:
If you’ve ever been curious about the world you live in, you’ve probably wondered why the sky is blue. It’s a question that most children ask at some point in their lives, but the answers that adults give them often don’t align with our physical reality. items.description:
In 1883, the British physicist Joseph John Thomson wrote his master’s thesis,  A Treatise on the Motion of Vortex Rings , exploring the fluid dynamics that govern the motion of phenomena like smoke rings and circular underwater vortices. items.title: NASA’s Hubble opens the earliest window into the young Milky Way
items.description:
The Milky Way, spanning over 100,000 light-years, is our galactic home.

items.description: In our Universe, in all directions and in all locations, there’s simply more “stuff” that space is full of everywhere we look.
